text: A shift
Face to face
To be the norm
To phase out
Overnight
A habit
To look back on
For good
It used to be the norm here.
The shift happened overnight.
Some conversations are better face to face.
They phased it out over two years.
When I look back on it, it seems strange.
I used to travel every month, and now I do not.
Every Monday we would meet at eight, whether there was anything to say or not.
I used to have an office with my name on the door.
I went to London in 2019, once, for four days.
It changed overnight, and it has not gone back.
That used to be the norm here. It is not any more.
Looking back on it, I am not sure it ever made sense.

Habits at work have a strange quality. While they last, they look like the only possible arrangement, and the moment they end nobody can quite explain why they were there. Think of the fax machine, or the eight-thirty meeting that existed so that everybody could report what they had written in an email the night before. People used to defend those things sincerely. They were not stupid and they were not lazy. The habit simply carried something real at the beginning, and then the reason quietly went away while the habit stayed. That is the useful question to ask about anything you still do every week. Not is this good, which is hard to answer, but this one: if it disappeared tomorrow, what exactly would we lose. If nobody in the room can say, you have found one.

Here is a small thing I dropped and never went back to. I used to print everything before a meeting. Every document, every set of numbers, one copy for each person, and I would do it the night before so that nothing went wrong in the morning. I told myself it was about being prepared, and part of it was. But the honest reason is that holding paper made me feel ready in a way that a screen did not, and that had nothing to do with the meeting at all. When it became impossible to do it, for about six months, I discovered that nobody had ever read them. Not once. What I actually needed was ten minutes of reading beforehand, and I had been buying that feeling with an hour of printing.
